newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia-Belarus deal a victory for Kremlin liberals.
newsitem.headline: Russia-Belarus deal a victory for Kremlin liberals.

text.p: "Sooner or later we will enter our common home," Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko said after signing a Union Treaty with Russia on Wednesday.
On the evidence of the document that Russian President Boris Yeltsin finally agreed to sign with him, it will be later.
The text of the treaty, as reported by Russian media, is replete with the sort of fine sentiments of Slavic brotherhood that play well with voters in both former Soviet republics.
But there is little of substance.

Wednesday's signing was thus less significant as a tightening of ties between ex-Soviet states than as a victory for the Russian government's new liberals in their first skirmish with the conservative old guard.
In some respects, the "union" is less demanding than a "community" accord signed exactly a year ago.

Both the community and union documents say Russia and Belarus remain sovereign independent states while striving, precisely how is unclear, to integrate their economies, legal systems, defence and foreign policies. The aim is to "raise living standards" and "strengthen brotherhood".
But the firm deadlines contained in last year's community treaty -- synchronising economic reforms by the end of 1997 for example -- do not appear in the union pact.

Kremlin sources said the nine-point treaty signed by the two presidents emerged after a fierce last-minute campaign by liberals, led by new First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, who fear Lukashenko's unreformed Soviet-era economy and authoritarian political style would be damaging to Russia.

"It was a brilliant victory by the reformist wing of Russia's political elite," Sergei Parkhomenko, editor of the liberal weekly Itogi, told Reuters. "It was a courageous and effective intrigue conducted by them over the last few days."
An earlier, 17-page draft treaty approved by Lukashenko last week after negotiations with more conservative Moscow officials may resurface in the form of the union "charter".
This "charter" is described in the treaty as an "integral part" of it -- but no details were spelled out.

The draft treaty, according to a copy obtained by Reuters earlier this week, was vague and raised potential conflicts with the Russian constitution. A text of the charter, expected to be based on this draft, is to be presented for debate this month.
Lukashenko, who has reinforced his popularity despite economic hardships in his country of 10 million by pushing hard for union with Moscow, was clearly disappointed on Wednesday.
"Preparations for the document unfortunately did not take place without bitter opposition," he said during the signing.

Former Belarus leader Stanislav Shushkevich told Ekho Moskvy radio: "I'm very glad that the energetic young people in the Russian leadership are able to continue the course of reforms and that reactionary circles in Russia will not be able to be reinforced by Belarus's communist regime."
"It's a great shame," Aman Tuleyev, the communist who is Russia's minister for relations with former Soviet states, said of Yeltsin's decision to sign only a much reduced treaty.

Chubais, 41, and his liberal allies, appointed in Yeltsin's government shake-up last month, have kept their opposition to the Belarus deal low key, partly because the idea of closer ties is generally popular with the Russian public.
But Chubais's fellow first deputy premier, 37-year-old Boris Nemtsov, said on Wednesday the new pact was "much more thought-out than before, thanks to intelligent people".

One Kremlin source said some of the conservatives who drafted the original Lukashenko-approved treaty could find their jobs threatened as Yeltsin, newly active after a long illness, tried to push harder to complete democratic, market reforms.
But the hallmark of the 66-year-old president's style over the past decade has been to maintain a balance among competing groups of supporters. He seems unlikely to change now.
